\chapter{Dog and Cat}
\label{ch:spanish-dog-and-cat}
\hlchaptermodality{48}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a dog and a cat in Spanish and say which of the two words still has no agreed origin.}

Say gato and perro, trace cattus back toward Egypt, then admit that perro — which pushed out the older can — has no settled etymology at all.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[gato]{gato — the word that travelled with the animal}

\label{lesson:ES-C32-gato}



\begin{quote}
Some etymologies can be followed all the way home. This one runs from your mouth back to ancient Egypt, and every step of it is documented.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{gato} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{cat}\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{cattus}. But \emph{cattus} was \textbf{not} Classical Latin's word for cat. That was \textbf{fēlēs}, which survives today only in the scientific name \emph{Felis catus} and in English \textbf{feline}.

\emph{Cattus} entered Latin \textbf{later}, arriving with the animal itself as domestic cats spread along \textbf{Roman trade routes} from where they were domesticated — \textbf{Egypt}, around 2000 BCE. The word is most likely \textbf{Afro-Asiatic} in origin (compare Nubian \textbf{kadis}, \textquotedblleft{}cat\textquotedblright{}).

So word and creature travelled together, out of Africa into Europe, and the newcomer pushed \emph{fēlēs} out almost everywhere: Spanish \emph{gato}, Italian \emph{gatto}, French \emph{chat}, Old Irish \emph{cat}, Welsh \emph{cath}, English \emph{cat}. When a thing arrives from abroad, its name usually arrives with it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el gato\textquotedblright{} — the cat
  \item the trail — \textquotedblleft{}kadis, cattus, gato\textquotedblright{}
  \item the word it replaced — \textquotedblleft{}fēlēs,\textquotedblright{} now only in \textquotedblleft{}feline\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was Classical Latin's actual word for cat, and where does it survive? (\textbf{Fēlēs} — in \emph{Felis catus} and English \emph{feline}.) Where did \emph{cattus} most likely come from? (An \textbf{Afro-Asiatic} word, travelling with the domesticated cat out of \textbf{Egypt}.) Next: the other animal in this chapter, whose history nobody can trace at all.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[perro]{perro — the word nobody can explain}

\label{lesson:ES-C32-perro}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Gato} could be traced all the way to Egypt. \textbf{Perro} is the opposite kind of word, and it is worth knowing that such words exist: completely ordinary, used a thousand times a day, and \textbf{nobody knows where it came from}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{perro} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{dog}\textquotedblright{}). Roll the \emph{rr}: \emph{PEH-rro}.

The word Spanish \textbf{should} have inherited is \textbf{canis} — the same root as English \textbf{canine}, French \emph{chien}, Italian \emph{cane}. And it did survive, as the now-archaic Spanish \textbf{can} (still readable in old poetry and in \emph{canino}). But at some point \emph{perro} pushed \emph{can} almost entirely out of everyday use — and \emph{perro} itself has no agreed origin.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Three serious proposals, none confirmed:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{proposal} & \textbf{the case for it} & \textbf{the problem} \\
\midrule
\textbf{onomatopoeia} — a growl, or a shepherd's call \emph{\textquotedblleft{}perr, perr\textquotedblright{}} & matches how herding calls become names elsewhere & no early written evidence \\
\textbf{pre-Roman Iberian substrate} & the \emph{-rro} ending is a known marker of likely pre-Latin words in Spanish & the substrate languages are barely recorded \\
Persian \emph{persus}, a hunting-dog breed & such breeds did spread in the late Empire & the sound match is loose \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Notice what makes this a \textbf{good} open question rather than a shrug: each proposal predicts different evidence, and the evidence needed simply has not survived. \emph{Perro} remains one of Spanish's genuinely unsolved puzzles, and a useful reminder that \textquotedblleft{}we don't know\textquotedblright{} is a real answer in etymology, not a gap in your notes.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el perro, el gato\textquotedblright{} — dog and cat
  \item \textquotedblleft{}can\textquotedblright{} — the archaic word \emph{perro} replaced, from Latin \emph{canis}
  \item the contrast — \textquotedblleft{}gato, traced to Egypt; perro, unsolved\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What archaic Spanish word did \emph{perro} replace, and what is its Latin source? (\textbf{Can}, from \textbf{canis} — the root of English \emph{canine}.) Does \emph{perro} have a confirmed etymology? (\textbf{No} — onomatopoeic, pre-Latin substrate and Persian proposals all remain unconfirmed.) And \emph{gato}'s origin, by contrast? (\textbf{Traceable} — Latin \emph{cattus}, probably Afro-Asiatic, travelling out of Egypt.)
\end{tcolorbox}
